title: TT-Bio benchmarks: biomolecular structure prediction, design and binding affinity on Tenstorrent hardware
subtitle: Eight structure-prediction models, two binder-design models and one binding-affinity model at 512 residues, measured on Tenstorrent Blackhole and on NVIDIA H200, B200 and A100.
notes: This file is the only place numbers are edited. index.html reads it and derives everything else.
Never write a derived value here. Server throughput, cost per hour and both throughput-per-dollar charts are computed in the page from s_per_fold, accelerators, price and power.

A row is published only when every processor column is measured. A model with a blank column waits in perf/page_rows_pending.json until its missing cells exist, because a half-measured row still draws a bar and reads as a claim. scripts/site_publish_guard.py enforces this, --strip holds a row and --restore publishes it.

One cell per model per platform, holding the fastest measured arm that passes parity against its own reference. Every Tenstorrent cell states which parity it holds: bit-exact, byte-identical, or a measured structural delta inside a bar that was fixed before the number existed. A cell with no measurement gets status 'blocked' and a reason. Do not fill it with an estimate.

The A100 appears twice: as a card, and as the DGX A100 640GB, the eight-GPU box NVIDIA sold that card in. The $175,000 that box carries is an assumed street price, not a vendor list price, and it is labelled as one everywhere it is used.
A design model carrying 'hidden': true keeps every measured cell here and is drawn nowhere. Delete that one line to publish the row again.

Every Tenstorrent cell states the board it was measured on. It inherits `measured_on` from its platform and overrides it only if it ran somewhere else. The column is priced as a p150a; the board that produced the number is a separate fact and is stated as one.

The embed block is measured but not published. All six rows carry "hidden": true and the page has no code that reads it, so the guard counts them out of the title, the subtitle and the meta description. site/README.md records what was run. Restoring the section means dropping the flags, putting the chart and the t-embed table back, and moving EXPECT_ROWS.embed in render_check.js in the same commit.

scope.description: CDK2 (PDB 1HCL) tandem-duplicated to 512 residues, one protein chain, no ligands, a fixed 35-sequence MSA.
scope.protocol: Warm folds, one prediction at a time on one accelerator, the same two input files on both sides, each model at its own recycle and sampling-step settings. Each Tenstorrent cell is that model's fastest arm that passes parity.
scope.split: Two readings of the same eight rows. Whole fold counts every second a user waits for on both sides. Device only strips the host work off both sides, and it is the reading that says what the silicon does. The Tenstorrent host seconds are inside the published cell on every row; the NVIDIA ones sit outside it on the five folding rows and inside it on RoseTTAFold3, PXDesign and Nesso-1, whose cells time host and device together. Every Tenstorrent host figure is an upper bound, so every device-only ratio here is a lower bound on the real device gap. This table is Blackhole against H200 only.
scope.gpu_generations: The B200 is not uniformly faster than the H200 on these workloads. Six rows go the H200's way by a clear margin: Boltz-2 by 10.2 %, OpenFold3 15.9 %, OpenBind-0 16.0 %, BoltzGen 27.2 %, ESMFold2-Fast 78.3 % and Nesso-1 84.0 %. PXDesign is the one row where the two are level, 0.7 % to the H200 against within-arm spreads of 5.1 % and 5.5 %. Every other row goes the B200's way. The B200 cells were re-measured on a config-identical machine and reproduce within 4.1 %, so the split is real. It is not the host: cutting the B200 box from 24 cores to 6 with taskset moves Boltz-2 by less than 1.5 % (8.285 / 8.163 / 8.192 s), and on single-threaded featurisation the B200 box's Xeon 8559C is 1.51x faster than the H200 box's Xeon 8480+ (8.275 s against 12.459 s on the same RoseTTAFold3 work), so the host difference runs toward the B200, not against it. The mechanism is saturation. Solving Boltz-2 at four recycle and sampling-step points on both cards gives 0.541 s per recycle on the B200 against 0.620 s on the H200, and 0.0288 s per sampling step against 0.0241 s: the B200 is the faster trunk, the H200 is the faster sampler. The published Boltz-2 cell is 70 % sampler on the B200 and 66 % on the H200, and the sampler phase draws 379 W of the B200's 1000 W limit at 68 % utilisation against 404 W of the H200's 700 W at 90 %. At 512 residues these workloads do not fill a B200. One packaging term was measured and it is small: cuEquivariance's Blackwell triangle-attention kernel ships only in the cu13 wheels and the published cells ran cu12; per call it is 2.69x faster, end to end it moves Boltz-2 by -2.76 % and BoltzGen the wrong way by +4.28 %.
scope.timed_region: Each cell times what that platform's own harness times, and the regions are not identical: every Tenstorrent number is a whole prediction call with featurisation and structure writing inside it, and on NVIDIA that is true of RoseTTAFold3 and effectively true of ESMFold2, but the Boltz-2, OpenFold3, Protenix-v2 and OpenDDE cells time the network forward and leave host work outside the timer. What they leave out is 0.24 s, 0.43 s, 0.62 s and 6.31 s per prediction, which makes those four ratios larger than a like-for-like comparison would. The host and device table gives both readings for every row.

cost_model.amortisation_basis: Four years is this page's assumption for how long an AI accelerator earns its keep: one year shorter than the general-purpose server life Amazon reports in its 10-Q, because an accelerator generation lasts about two years. A shorter window favours the cheaper box, so the range below brackets it.
cost_model.utilisation: The machine predicts continuously, so every hour of ownership is an hour of throughput.
cost_model.formula: Throughput per dollar, with the DGX H200 set to 1.00x, on two bases. Purchase price: predictions per hour / price, with no amortisation window, because the window cancels from that ratio. Total cost of ownership: predictions per hour / cost per hour, where cost per hour = price / (4 x 8766 h) + power kW x $/kWh.
cost_model.sensitivity: Shift the window to 3 or 6 years, or the rate to the 13.54 c/kWh US commercial tariff, and the Tenstorrent figure moves between 2.47x and 3.71x. It does not invert.

models.name: OpenDDE

p150a.parity: 0.867 A CA RMSD on the 298-residue control, outside the 0.35 A bar this cell fixed before the measurement. One disordered loop carries the whole excess: trim the worst 5 % of atoms and the two arms agree to 0.339 A, which is what this control read before the token-bucket pad shipped on by default (see ref).
p150a.ref: Median of three warm folds on one Blackhole AI Processor, 82.372 / 82.393 / 82.422 s, spread 0.050 s, measured uninstrumented on the shipped path, cold fold discarded. The 82.942 s this cell carried before is the same measurement without the host-side glue: the relative-position one-hot is now scattered into an fp32 result instead of built from int64 one-hots and an int64 concatenation, and the trunk-to-structural pair copy stays in the bf16 the device already held. Both are bit-exact and both are host time, worth 0.498 s at the fold with the CIF digest unchanged and the device wall flat to inside its own spread. This is the one cell that is not bit-exact against the reference: the triangle-attention matmul folds its contraction in twelve-tile blocks, worth one bf16 unit in the last place, so the CIF digest moves 50aa1e46583bd5a8 to 357c67003bb738ac and plDDT 0.754131 to 0.754110. The structural cost is measured on a monomeric 298-residue control, apo human CDK2, because this fixture's two domains hinge freely and saturate the metric. It read 0.3248 A Kabsch CA when this cell was measured and reads 0.867 A on the shipped path now that the token-bucket pad is on by default, which pads that control's residue axis from 298 to 320. The control saturates too: the entire deviation is CDK2's activation loop, residues 157 to 167, disordered in the apo form and sitting at plDDT 0.49 against 0.84 for the rest of the chain, and trimming the worst 5 % of atoms returns 0.339 A. Whole-chain plDDT is 0.822 with the pad against 0.802 without it. The re-measurement ran on a p300c card rather than this cell's p150a, and reproduced the old number in its own condition first, 0.3087 A with the pad off. The pad costs this cell no time: eight interleaved pairs at this protocol on a p150a card read -0.101 s for it. The byte-identical arm at the same two matmul settings returns 88.61 s. The plDDT and digests above are the 2026-08-14 measurement and no longer describe main. Four changes moved this fixture after it, all measured commit by commit on one card at this protocol. Two are correctness fixes: 1ea1e6f3 (08-17) repaired a pair-init bias reshape that split a TILE row axis on a structural-token count that is not a multiple of 32, worth +0.0164, and 4e3d922a (08-22) removed an OuterProductMean bias-scale term of proj_o.bias * (1 - 1/n_msa) that the reference does not have, worth -0.0418 and taking the trunk's z against the CPU reference from 0.947762 to 0.991964 PCC. Two are smaller: 01f21dfb (08-24) turned the token-bucket pad on by default and raised TOKEN_PAD_MULTIPLE from 32 to 64, worth -0.000140, and 86df9db9 (08-27) stopped forcing a core grid on the 128-wide pair-conditioning projections to clear an intermittent ttnn multicast-matmul deadlock, worth -0.000091 and reproducible at main tip with PROTENIX_PAIRCOND_MM_FORCE_GRID=1. Main now reads plDDT 0.725015 with CIF digest 5012ef53b697f57f on qb2, the same card class the digests above were taken on. Structure quality is better, not worse: the 08-14 code folds this fixture with 19 backbone gaps over 5 A and 9.50 % of heavy atoms clashing, main folds it with 0 gaps and 0.56 %, scored by the release gate's own geometry harness. The confidence fell because the corrupted pair track was inflating it. The timing in this cell is unaffected and was re-read inside its own spread.

models.name: SaProt 35M
models.note: At 16.6 seq/s this row is slower than SaProt 1.3B at 23.4 on the same card, which reads as a page bug and is not one. SaProt 35M has a head dim of 24 (hidden 480 over 20 heads), neither tile-aligned nor aligned with the fused on-device rotary kernel, so the port splits heads, applies RoPE on host in fp32 and pads 24 to 32 on host, once per layer. That costs 35.2 ms per layer against 4.5-4.7 ms per layer for the two larger sizes at hidden 1280, and it is also why this is the widest-spread Tenstorrent row here at 13.0 %. Documented in docs/saprot-parity.md under "35M host-side RoPE path"; a fix is proposed, not landed.

caveats: Rows are not a cross-model ranking. Boltz-2 and OpenFold3 do 3 recycles where ESMFold2, Protenix-v2 and OpenDDE do 10, because that is what each ships. Compare a model to itself across hardware. BoltzGen returns a binder design, not a prediction; its bars share an axis with the prediction models but not a unit.

The A100 ran every cell on this page, on the same fixtures. Its host is an AMD EPYC 7513 where the H200 and B200 boxes were Intel Xeon, which matters for the dispatch-bound trunks and is not corrected for, and the RoseTTAFold3 cell ran later on an EPYC 7763 at the same 30.7 vCPU quota. PXDesign's A100 cell is a third box, an EPYC 7713 at a 30.72 vCPU quota, picked to hold that quota because 3.1 s of its number is host featurisation.

RoseTTAFold3's NVIDIA cells carry the widest spreads on this page, and host featurisation is why: host prep varies far more run to run than device work does, so raising the H200 cell from three folds to eight moved its median 3.6 % and left the spread where it was.

The Tenstorrent host figures in the host and device table were measured on a box that was running three other jobs. Contention only adds host time, so each one is an upper bound, and every device-only ratio built from one is a lower bound on the real device gap.

The NVIDIA host figures for the five folding rows come from one rented H200 with the same Xeon Platinum 8480+ and the same vCPU quota as the published cells. Four of the five sessions reproduced their published cell within 2.3 %. The ESMFold2 session did not, and its figure rests on the shape of that harness's timed region instead; the cell note says so. RoseTTAFold3, PXDesign and Nesso-1 need no such session, because their cells time host and device together and the split is read straight out of the published number. B200 and A100 host work is measured only where a row splits its cell that way, and no figure is carried across platforms.

Every Tenstorrent number on this page was measured on tt-quietbox2, on one Blackhole AI Processor of a p300c board, not on the p150a the column is named and priced for. Tenstorrent specifies the same 120 Tensix cores and the same 32 GB at 512 GB/s per processor on both, and does not sell the p300c separately or publish a price for it, so the p150a is the only part of the two with a price to compute against. They are not interchangeable in practice: the board measured here exposes an 11x10 Tensix grid where our p150a reads 13x10, both read off the hardware, and its host is an AMD Ryzen 7 9700X where our p150a box runs an AMD EPYC 8124P, which matters for the dispatch-bound trunks. No fold has been measured on the p150a, so this page states no direction for the difference. Two PXDesign checks did run on a p150a and neither is published as a number: they are A/Bs of that card against itself, for drift across commits and for fp32 against bf16, and both are described in the PXDesign Tenstorrent cell.

PXDesign's NVIDIA cells are the only ones on this page measured on torch 2.7.1 with CUDA 12.8; every other row's NVIDIA cells are torch 2.3.1 on CUDA 12.1. PXDesign needed the move because CUDA 12.1 emits no sm_100 device code, so its B200 could not otherwise run what its H200 measured, and a row is only worth reading if all of it comes from one stack. Within the PXDesign row the three NVIDIA cells are on that one stack. Across rows they are not, which is another reason caveat 1 applies: compare a model to itself.
